name: matchedfilter (formerly peak-fft)
language: C core with Python bindings; GPU kernels in Slang (Vulkan/Metal)
baseline: FFTW (inverse transform only, timed through pyFFTW); on GPU rocFFT / MLX FFT inverse-only references
workload: Batched matched filtering (frequency-domain product, inverse FFT and peak scan) of 16 data spectra x 512 templates x 4096-point complex64 transforms, one CPU thread, timed against FFTW doing only the inverse FFT of the same batch.
claimed_speedup: Milliseconds per batch, FFTW inverse-only vs matchedfilter peak-only: Ryzen 9 5950X 63.63 vs 34.27; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 69.54 vs 20.68; Apple M2 252.55 vs 57.84; Core i5-13500H 44.96 vs 35.49. Full-output mode: 52.23, 35.12, 68.75 and 56.24 ms respectively (slower than FFTW on the i5-13500H). Hierarchical screening: 3.95, 3.12, 6.28 and 4.69 ms at fd=0.01. Peak-only is 1.86x, 3.36x, 4.37x and 1.27x faster than FFTW's inverse-only time on those four CPUs (derived from page data). GPU (Radeon 8060S): FFT-only reference 2.58 ms vs peak-only 0.71 ms.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Radeon 8060S); Ryzen 5 5500U; Intel Core i5-13500H; Apple M2; Xeon Platinum 8260 (VM); Xeon E5-2698 v3 (shared, contended node)
tradeoffs: Not a general-purpose FFT. It fuses the spectral product, inverse FFT and peak search for matched-filter searches. Peak-only sizes are powers of two from 64 to 1,048,576 on CPU; full-output sizes are powers of two from 1,024 to 4,194,304. Single precision (complex64) only, one CPU thread per filter. The main interface is a pip-installable Python package over a C core, so use from C++ means linking the C code directly. Hierarchical mode needs calibration files and trades a false-dismissal budget for speed. The README calls it alpha software with an unstable API.
caveats: First-party numbers from a very young repo. FFTW and the GPU FFT references time only the inverse transform, so the comparison is between unequal amounts of work (the page says so itself); the gain comes from fusion and peak-only output, not from a faster FFT kernel. Full-output mode is slower than FFTW on the Core i5-13500H and on the Haswell node. The page flags the Haswell node as contended (its full-output and hierarchical rows are indicative only) and the Xeon VM as least stable. FFTW version, planner flags and thread count, and the compile flags used for matchedfilter, are not stated, so tier C. The interactive benchmark pages at ahnitz.github.io are not reachable from this environment; numbers come from the repo's own measurement document and README. The repo was renamed from peak-fft, and its docs mention agent handoffs and plan files, so treat claims as unreviewed.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch restricted to code hosts for 'FFT library README "faster than FFTW" benchmark AVX2 radix-4 split-radix single header' returned ahnitz/peak-fft, which redirects to ahnitz/matchedfilter

name: GPU_FFT (Raspberry Pi VideoCore IV, hello_fft)
language: C with VideoCore QPU assembly kernels
baseline: FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE) running on the Raspberry Pi 1 ARM CPU
workload: Single-precision complex power-of-two FFTs from 2^8 to 2^22 points: per-transform runtime on the BCM2835 GPU (batch of 1 and 10) against FFTW_MEASURE on the same Pi 1.
claimed_speedup: Doc text: 'ten times more data throughput than is possible on the 700 MHz ARM of the Pi 1'. Per-transform milliseconds, GPU_FFT (batch 1) vs FFTW_MEASURE: 2^8 0.033 vs 0.092; 2^12 0.25 vs 3.0; 2^15 3.5 vs 31; 2^16 7.0 vs 83; 2^20 194 vs 1600; 2^22 786 vs 8800. That is 2.8x, 12x, 8.9x, 11.9x, 8.2x and 11.2x (derived from page data).
hardware: Raspberry Pi 1 (BCM2835, 700 MHz ARM, VideoCore IV GPU, L2 cache enabled)
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars (raspberrypi/userland, archived 2025-08-27); shipped as the hello_fft demo with Raspbian
tradeoffs: Tied to the BCM2835 VideoCore IV 3D hardware and the Raspberry Pi mailbox device (the demo runs under sudo). Single-precision only, power-of-two lengths from 256 to 4,194,304, and a transpose helper for 2D. Per the doc, accuracy is 0.33 to 1.5 ppm rms and FFTW is still one order of magnitude more accurate. C API, so callable from C++.
caveats: First-party table from the library's own doc file (release 3.0, 2015), measured on 2015-era Pi 1 hardware. It compares GPU offload against a CPU FFTW on the same SoC; the FFTW version, precision, build flags and thread count are not stated and no compiler is given. The benchmark code (hello_fft.c) is in the repo but no compiler or flags are recorded. The repo is archived and deprecated by its maintainers. The author's blog page for GPU_FFT was not opened; all numbers come from gpu_fft.txt. The last commit date is for the hello_fft directory.
found_via: Blogs / talks: recalled the well-known Raspberry Pi GPU_FFT blog and library; opened hello_fft/gpu_fft.txt in raspberrypi/userland. The blog page itself was not opened.

name: PocketFFT (C++ header-only), independent benchmark
baseline: KissFFT (also FFTW_ESTIMATE and FFTW_MEASURE, Intel MKL as reference)
workload: Independent shootout by the project-gemmi author: 1D complex and real transforms, 2D, and 3D complex-to-complex and real-to-complex (256^3 and other sizes), single precision except the C pocketfft in the 1D tables, timed with their own benchmark programs.
claimed_speedup: 3D c2c 256x256x256: pocketfft 264 ms vs KissFFT 785 ms, FFTW est. 730 ms, FFTW meas. 162 ms, MKL 155 ms. 3D r2c 256x256x256: pocketfft AVX 97 ms vs KissFFT 436 ms, FFTW est. 219 ms, FFTW meas. 98 ms, MKL 61 ms. 1D c2c n=512 with SIMD disabled: pocketfft 4009 ns vs KissFFT 6553 ns. Plan creation n=512: pocketfft 1274 ns vs FFTW meas. 25610 ns. Ratios (derived from page data): about 3.0x over KissFFT on 3D c2c, 4.5x on 3D r2c, 1.6x on 1D c2c without SIMD; parity with FFTW_MEASURE on 3D r2c with AVX; slower than FFTW_MEASURE and MKL on 3D c2c.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8 -O3 (Clang 8 also tried; the page says pocketfft is about 12% faster with Clang 8)
hardware: Intel Core i7-5600U (listing shows 4 CPUs at 3200 MHz; L1d 32K x2, L2 256K x2, L3 4096K)
stars_or_usage: 158 stars (mreineck/pocketfft); the gemmi README says NumPy (from 1.17) and SciPy (from 1.4.0) adopted PocketFFT
tradeoffs: Vectorizes only multi-dimensional transforms or batches of 1D transforms, and uses GCC/Clang vector extensions rather than intrinsics, so top speed needs GCC or Clang. Very cheap plan creation and a small header-only footprint.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known). Benchmark repo last updated 2022-06-21 on a 2015 laptop CPU; the 1D tables use the double-precision C pocketfft against single-precision rivals, and the author was migrating to the cpp branch. The compiler is stated in the 1D section, not repeated for every 3D table. FFTW was Ubuntu 18.04 binaries, not rebuilt. Against FFTW_MEASURE and MKL pocketfft is slower or at parity, so the clear win is over KissFFT and FFTW_ESTIMATE.

name: muFFT, independent benchmark
workload: Independent shootout by the project-gemmi author: single-precision 1D complex and real-to-complex transforms (n=256..512) and 2D complex 256x256, with SIMD enabled and disabled.
claimed_speedup: 2D c2c 256x256: mufft 259 us vs FFTW est. 1197 us and FFTW meas. 306 us. 1D r2c n=512: mufft 511 ns vs FFTW est. 814 ns and FFTW meas. 681 ns. Ratios (derived from page data): 4.6x and 1.18x on 2D c2c; 1.59x and 1.33x on 1D r2c. On 1D c2c muFFT is slower than FFTW_MEASURE (n=256: 325 vs 274 ns; n=512: 719 vs 588 ns) and about level with FFTW_ESTIMATE.
tradeoffs: Only 1D and 2D transforms, sizes limited to what its radix codelets support (the shootout shows n/a for n=384, 480 and 480x480), no 3D, single precision only in the shootout's feature table. Separate no-SIMD, SSE, SSE3 and AVX codelets, about 80 kB of binary.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known). Mixed result: wins over FFTW on 2D c2c 256x256 and 1D r2c n=512 but loses to FFTW_MEASURE on 1D c2c. 2015-era laptop CPU, benchmark repo last touched 2022-06-21, FFTW from Ubuntu 18.04 binaries. The GitHub page lists both MIT and GPL-2.0, so check which files carry the GPL before copying.
